title: Levered DCF
objectives: Answer out loud: When would you use a levered DCF?

steps.body: Levered FCF = net income + D&A − CapEx − increase in NWC − mandatory debt repayment + new borrowing.
Result = equity value directly (no bridge needed).

blocks.title: Why are levered DCFs rarely used?
blocks.teaser: You have to project every debt issuance and repayment, and changing leverage changes the cost of equity each year.
blocks.body: You have to project every debt issuance and repayment, and changing leverage changes the cost of equity each year. It's more complex and assumption-heavy than the unlevered version.

blocks.title: When would you use one?
blocks.teaser: For financial institutions (where debt is operational and EV doesn't apply), or when the capital structure is fixed and known, as in an LBO.
blocks.body: For financial institutions (where debt is operational and EV doesn't apply), or when the capital structure is fixed and known, as in an LBO.

blocks.prompt: When is a levered DCF most appropriate?

options.text: For financial institutions, or when the capital structure is fixed and known

blocks.explanation: Levered DCFs fit banks (where EV doesn't apply) and cases like an LBO where the debt schedule is fixed and known.

blocks.title: Should levered and unlevered DCFs give the same equity value?
blocks.teaser: In theory, yes, if all assumptions are consistent.
blocks.body: In theory, yes, if all assumptions are consistent. In practice they differ, because keeping leverage and discount rates consistent across years is hard.
